desc_b: The University of New Mexico (UNM) is a public R1 research university with nationally recognized strengths in nuclear engineering, radiochemistry, environmental engineering, earth and planetary sciences, and materials science. UNM is particularly well known for its work on naturally occurring radioactive materials (NORM), legacy uranium mining impacts, and environmental remediation in arid and semi-arid regions. UNM’s research portfolio is deeply connected to real-world radioactive and mineral waste challenges, supported by long-standing engagement with DOE national laboratories, federal agencies, and regional industry. desc_a: Sandia National Laboratories is a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) National Laboratory primarily funded by the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) and operated by National Technology & Engineering Solutions of Sandia (NTESS). Sandia’s core mission is to apply advanced science and engineering to solve complex national-scale problems, particularly where safety, security, reliability, and long-term performance are critical. Unlike discovery-oriented national labs, Sandia is internationally recognized for its strength in applied engineering, systems integration, materials durability, radiation effects, and risk-informed decision-making. It plays a central role in translating laboratory science into deployable, regulator-ready technologies, especially in domains involving hazardous materials, radioactive elements, and long-term environmental stewardship. For the NutriCrops phosphogypsum and radionuclide elimination challenge, Sandia’s value lies in its ability to engineer, test, validate, and de-risk treatment systems, waste forms, and containment strategies under real-world operational and regulatory constraints.
desc_b: SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory is a U.S. Department of Energy national laboratory operated by Stanford University. It specializes in advanced photon science, accelerator science, materials characterization, nuclear science, and high-resolution imaging technologies. SLAC is home to world-leading facilities including: Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL) Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS) These facilities allow atomic-scale and molecular-scale characterization of materials, including radioactive materials, mineral phases, and chemical bonding environments. While SLAC does not focus directly on phosphate processing, it plays a critical role in: Characterizing radionuclide binding mechanisms Understanding mineral phase transformations Validating immobilization chemistry Advanced materials structural analysis SLAC is a high-credibility scientific validation partner.

Florida is the only U.S. jurisdiction where PG reuse is being cautiously reopened at the federal level, making it the most deployment-relevant hub for NutriCrops.

Unlike discovery-oriented national labs, Sandia is internationally recognized for its strength in applied engineering, systems integration, materials durability, radiation effects, and risk-informed decision-making. desc_a: Duke University is a major private research university in Durham, North Carolina with world-class interdisciplinary research across environmental science, geochemistry, engineering, and nuclear sciences. Within Duke, several laboratories and research units focus on occurrence, behavior, measurement, and impacts of radionuclides in the environment, including naturally occurring radioactive materials (NORM) and technologically enhanced NORM (TENORM) such as those found in phosphogypsum.
desc_b: Iowa State University (ISU) is a major public land-grant research university in Ames, Iowa with a broad science and engineering portfolio. It is distinctive among U.S. universities because it hosts Ames National Laboratory — a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) national lab co-located on campus — creating a highly integrated research ecosystem spanning materials science, nuclear and radiological chemistry, environmental science, and analytical technology. ISU has research strengths across engineering (materials, environmental, civil), chemistry, physics, and earth sciences, with faculty involved in measurement science and environmental systems that may relate indirectly to radionuclides and TENORM.

desc_b: The National Energy Technology Laboratory (NETL) is a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratory focused on applied research, engineering, and technology development to enable secure, sustainable, and environmentally responsible energy and industrial systems. Unlike Office of Science labs, NETL is mission- and deployment-oriented, with deep expertise in process engineering, materials durability, environmental management, carbon and mineral systems, and large-scale pilot validation. NETL’s work sits squarely at the interface of science, engineering, and deployment, making it highly relevant for industrial waste valorization, large-volume byproduct management, and regulatory-aligned technology scale-up—all central to phosphogypsum challenges.

desc_a: Idaho National Laboratory (INL) is the U.S. DOE’s lead national laboratory for nuclear energy research, with deep capabilities in nuclear fuel cycle chemistry, radiochemistry, waste processing, materials behavior, and deployment-grade engineering under strict regulatory frameworks. INL specializes in translating nuclear and radiochemical science into operational, regulated, and scalable systems. For Nutri-Crops, INL is particularly valuable where phosphogypsum (PG) is treated as a nuclear-adjacent material (NORM/TENORM): bridging radiochemistry, systems engineering, waste classification, and long-term performance.
desc_b: Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) is a leading DOE national laboratory with globally recognized capabilities in chemical separations, radiochemistry, environmental fate and transport, materials science, and systems integration. PNNL is especially strong at the interface of chemistry, environment, and deployment, making it a natural complement to ORNL and INL. For Nutri-Crops, PNNL provides separation science, environmental validation, and system-level deployment insight for phosphogypsum (PG) and other nuclear-adjacent industrial residues.
